title: Rebase Conflicts
description: Diagnose, resolve, and prevent conflicts during interactive rebases and branch rebases.

data.text: Conflicts during rebase are common and normal. They happen when Git cannot automatically combine your changes with the target branch. Understanding how rebase conflicts work — and how they differ from merge conflicts — helps you resolve them quickly and confidently.

Merge conflicts happen once and produce a single merge commit. Rebase conflicts happen sequentially — for each commit in your branch, Git tries to replay it on top of main and stops at the first conflict. This means you may resolve the same area of code multiple times during a long rebase.

data.title: Rebase conflicts are not binary
data.text: A rebase conflict on commit 3 does not mean the entire branch is broken. It means commit 3 cannot be applied cleanly on top of main. Resolve it and continue — later commits may apply without issue.

When a rebase conflict occurs, Git pauses and tells you exactly which commit and file caused the conflict. Use git status to see the conflicted files and git log to understand what changed in the conflicting commit.

data.title: Diagnose a rebase conflict
data.code:
# See which commit caused the conflict
git rebase --show-current-patch

# See list of conflicted files
git status

# See what the current (ours) version looks like
git diff

# See what the incoming (theirs) version looks like
git diff --theirs

# See the common ancestor (base)
git diff --base

# See the commit that is being applied
git log -1

data.text: Edit each conflicted file to resolve the conflict markers. Stage the resolved files with git add, then run git rebase --continue. If you realize the conflict cannot be resolved cleanly, use git rebase --abort to return to the original branch state.

data.title: Resolve a rebase conflict and continue
data.code:
# 1. See conflicted files
git status

# 2. Edit the conflicted file(s)
# Remove conflict markers and keep the correct code

# 3. Stage the resolved files
git add src/auth/LoginService.cs

# 4. Continue the rebase
git rebase --continue

# 5. If you need to skip the current commit entirely
git rebase --skip

# 6. If you want to give up and start over
git rebase --abort

items: Rebase frequently — smaller batches have fewer conflicts
Keep feature branches short — rebase daily onto main
Coordinate with teammates on overlapping files
Use feature flags so incomplete features do not block integration
Split large commits so conflicts are isolated to one area

data.text: Git supports external merge tools for resolving conflicts. Configure your preferred tool (VS Code, Beyond Compare, KDiff3, etc.) and invoke it with git mergetool during a conflict.

data.title: Configure and use a merge tool
data.code:
# Configure VS Code as the merge tool
git config --global merge.tool vscode
git config --global mergetool.vscode.cmd 'code --wait $MERGED'

# Launch the merge tool during a conflict
git mergetool

# After resolving, stage and continue
git add src/auth/LoginService.cs
git rebase --continue

# Disable the tool prompt in the future
git config --global mergetool.prompt false

items.question: Why do I get the same conflict twice during rebase?
items.answer: Two of your commits modify the same area. Git replays each commit in sequence and conflicts on both. After resolving once, fixup the second commit or squash both commits before rebasing.

items.question: Can I use git checkout to resolve a conflict?
items.answer: Yes. git checkout --theirs <file> takes the incoming version; git checkout --ours <file> takes your version. Useful for binary files or trivial conflicts.

items.question: Is there a way to skip all remaining conflicts?
items.answer: git rebase --skip drops the current conflicting commit. Use it only when you are certain the commit is not needed.

items.question: What if I lose work during rebase?
items.answer: Use git reflog to find the original branch tip and recover: git reset --hard HEAD@{n}. The reflog tracks every branch movement.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Rebase conflicts happen sequentially — one per commit that cannot be applied
Use git diff --theirs and git diff --base to see conflicting versions
Resolve, stage, and continue — or abort to return to the original state
Prevent conflicts by rebasing frequently and keeping branches short
Use git mergetool to resolve conflicts with an external visual tool
